questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 3 is at least 3, so "high"; 1 matches neither check, so "low". The arrow function takes types in the same places as a normal function: 6 / 2 is 3.

questions.q: With strict on, what does tsc say about this function?
questions.explain: TypeScript cannot guess what callers will pass. Without a type the parameter would silently be any, and strict turns that into error TS7006. Give it a type, such as task: Task.
options: Nothing: TypeScript infers task from how it is used

questions.q: Why does tsc reject this function?
questions.explain: The return type makes the compiler check every path. Falling off the end returns undefined. Add return false; at the end, or write return status === "done";.
options: A function with a return type must not use if
When the status is not "done", it returns undefined, which is not a boolean

questions.q: TypeScript can infer a function's return type. Why is writing it still a good habit for exported functions?
questions.explain: With a written return type, the compiler compares every return against your promise. Without it, a wrong inferred type only shows up where some other file uses the result.
options: The code runs faster with a written return type
A mistake is then reported inside the function, not at some distant caller
Exported functions cannot use inference at all

questions.explain: Passing undefined counts as leaving the argument out, so the default 1 is used. That lets you skip priority and still pass a note.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The left-out note is undefined, so ?? uses "-". An empty string is a real value, so ?? keeps it; || would have replaced it.

questions.q: Inside function formatTask(title: string, note?: string), what is the type of note?
questions.explain: An optional parameter may be left out, and then it is undefined. So you must check it before using it as a string, for example with note === undefined or ??.

questions.q: Inside function formatTask(title: string, priority: number = 1), what is the type of priority?
questions.explain: A default parameter is optional for the caller, but inside the function it always has a value. That is the difference from note?: string.
options: number: callers may leave it out, but the default fills it in
number | undefined, so you must check it first

questions.q: Which function does tsc reject?
questions.explain: Optional and default parameters must come after the required ones. In c, a required parameter follows an optional one, which tsc reports as an error.

questions.q: For function formatTask(title: string, priority: number = 1, note?: string): string, which call does tsc accept?
questions.explain: formatTask takes 1 to 3 arguments, and the second must be a number. The others are missing title, pass a string as the priority, or pass 4 arguments.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The rest parameter ...tags collects the extra arguments into a string[]. With no extra arguments it is an empty array, not undefined.
options:
Buy milk home shop
Call Ada undefined

questions.q: What does the type (task: Task) => boolean describe?
questions.explain: A function type looks like an arrow function without a body. Functions are values in JavaScript, so they have types, and you can name one: type TaskFilter = (task: Task) => boolean.
options: A boolean value computed from a task
A function that takes a task and returns a boolean
A task whose properties are all booleans
An arrow function that has already been called

questions.q: Why does const isOpen: TaskFilter = (task) => !task.done; give no "implicitly has an 'any' type" error?
questions.explain: This is contextual typing: the type comes from where the function is used. It is also why tasks.filter((task) => ...) never needs an annotation.
options: The variable's type TaskFilter already says what task is, so TypeScript fills it in
TypeScript looks at task.done and guesses the type
Parameters of arrow functions are unknown by default

questions.q: The type is onEach: (task: Task, index: number) => void. Which callback does tsc accept?
questions.explain: A callback may take fewer parameters than the type lists; JavaScript simply drops the extra arguments. But the parameters it does take must have the right types, and it cannot ask for more than the caller gives.

questions.q: The callback type returns void, but the callback returns a number. What does this print?
questions.explain: push returns a number, and that is allowed: a void return type means "the result is ignored", not "must return nothing". The pushes still happen.

questions.q: tsc prints a long, three-line error about a callback whose index parameter has the wrong type. Where do you usually find the root cause?
questions.explain: Read long errors from the bottom up. The last line is the root cause, and each line above it adds context: which argument, which parameter.
options: On the last line, for example Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'string'
In the file named in the error

questions.q: This function returns a Task or undefined. What return type do you write?
questions.explain: An async function always returns a promise. Promise<T> names the type of the value it gives when done. Inside, you return a plain task; async wraps it.

questions.q: loadTask returns Promise<Task | undefined>. What is the type of task in const task = await loadTask(1);?
questions.explain: await unwraps the promise and gives you the value inside. It may still be undefined, so you check it before reading task.title.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: await gives the string inside each promise. No task has id 2, so task?.title is undefined and ?? picks the fallback text.

questions.q: Plain JavaScript, with a missing await. What does this print?
questions.explain: task is a promise object, and a promise has no title property, so JavaScript quietly gives undefined. In TypeScript this is an error.
options: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'title')

questions.q: In TypeScript, loadTask returns Promise<Task> and you write const task = loadTask(1); console.log(task.title);. What happens?
questions.explain: Forgetting await is the classic async bug. TypeScript knows task is a Promise<Task>, which has no title, and even suggests the fix.
options: tsc reports Property 'title' does not exist on type 'Promise<Task>' and asks if you forgot await
It prints Buy milk, because TypeScript waits automatically

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Calling an async function runs its body right away, up to the first await, so inside prints before after. The call returns a Promise<string>, and await takes out "hi".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The jobs run one after another, in the order of the array, and each result is awaited before it is pushed. So the strings come out in the order the jobs were given.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: No task has id 9, so find(9) is undefined. The array form always returns an array: ids 1 and 2 match, 9 does not, and an empty list of ids gives an empty array.

questions.q: With the two overloads find(id: number): Task | undefined and find(ids: number[]): Task[], what is the type of find([1, 2])?
questions.explain: Callers see only the overload signatures, and TypeScript picks the one that matches the argument. So find([1, 2]).length needs no check. The wide type belongs to the implementation, which callers cannot use directly.

questions.q: label returns a string whether you pass a number or a string id. What should you write?
questions.explain: Overloads are for when the return type depends on the input. When it does not, a union parameter is simpler. The lesson says: use overloads rarely.
options: Two overloads, one for each input
One signature with a union parameter: function label(id: number | string): string
Two functions with the same name in different files

questions.explain: Copying first keeps the caller's array unchanged, which is what readonly promises. tsc reports tasks.sort as an error.

The spread makes the sort faster

questions.q: In the retry helper, why is it return await job(); inside the try, and not just return job();?
questions.explain: The catch only sees the error if the promise is awaited inside the try. Returning the promise hands the rejection to the caller and skips the retry.
options: Without await, a rejected promise is returned instead of caught, so the loop never retries
They behave the same; await is only for readability

questions.q: With type Notify = (userId: number, message: string) => Promise<void>, which line does tsc accept?
questions.explain: The id must be a number, both arguments are required, and notify returns a Promise<void>, not a string. Awaiting a correct call is fine.

questions.q: Finish isFinished so it returns a boolean on every path: true for "done", false for anything else. The program should print true false.
questions.explain: return status === "done"; returns a boolean on every path. Returning true only inside an if would fall off the end, and tsc reports TS2366.

questions.q: Finish formatTask. priority defaults to 1, and note is optional: add - and the note only when there is one. The program should print Buy milk [P1] and then Call Ada [P2] - after 5pm.
questions.explain: Inside the function, priority is always a number thanks to the default, but note is string | undefined. Check it before adding it to the text.

questions.q: Write sumHours with a rest parameter, so it takes any number of hour values and returns their sum. Replace the parameter list and write the body. The program should print 0 2 6.5.
questions.explain: ...hours: number[] collects every argument into an array, which is empty when nothing is passed. So sumHours() returns 0 without any special case.

questions.q: Write two filters of type TaskFilter: isOpen (not done) and isUrgent (priority 3 or more). The program should print [ 'Fix login bug' ].
questions.explain: Thanks to contextual typing, task needs no annotation: the type TaskFilter already says it is a Task, so task.done and task.priority are checked.

questions.q: Finish countWhere: it takes the tasks and a callback, and returns how many tasks the callback says true for. The program should print 2 1.
questions.explain: Call the callback for each task and count the true answers. tasks.filter(test).length is a one-line version; filter is allowed on a readonly array because it does not change it.

questions.q: Finish forEachOpen: call onEach with each task that is not done and its position in the array. The program should print 0 Buy milk and then 2 File taxes.
questions.explain: The callback's type is on the parameter, so the compiler checks that you call it with a Task and a number. forEach gives you both.

questions.q: Write the comparer byTitle (A to Z, with localeCompare) and finish sortTasks so it returns a sorted copy. The program should print [ 'Call Ada', 'Fix login bug', 'Water plants' ] and then Water plants.
questions.explain: a.title.localeCompare(b.title) sorts A to Z. [...tasks] copies first, so the original array (still starting with Water plants) is not changed.
questions.expected:
[ 'Call Ada', 'Fix login bug', 'Water plants' ]
Water plants

questions.q: Finish titleOrDefault: await the task, and return its title, or task N not found. The program should print Buy milk and then task 2 not found.
questions.explain: await loadTask(id) has the type Task | undefined. Without await, task would be a promise, and tsc would ask whether you forgot to await it.

questions.q: Finish runInOrder: run the jobs one after another and return their results in order. The program should print [ 'email sent', 'log written' ].
questions.explain: Call each job and await its promise before pushing. Pushing job() without await would push promises, and tsc would refuse a Promise<string> in a string[].

questions.q: Finish retry: call job; if it rejects, try again, up to attempts times in total, then throw the last error. The job below fails twice and then works, so the program should print connected after 3 calls.
questions.explain: Use return await job() inside try, so a rejection is caught and the loop tries again. Keep the error as unknown, and throw it after the last attempt.
